# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.

- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,

  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the

  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style

- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

  and the preview HTML are regenerated server-side at request time.
- **get_project_status** — Text-only status check for an in-flight or finished

16	                                         Introduction
17	                                              An athlete’s health and availability to train and compete at an optimal performance
18	                                         level is a growing focus for professional sports organizations. Back-to-back competitions
19	                                         with limited recovery time, along with travelling across multiple time zones, are inherent
20	                                         challenges [1]. Studies suggest that a higher rate of injuries are sustained during the
21	                                         pre-season and during competitions [2]. These injuries include, but are not limited to,
22	                                         muscle strains [3], tendinopathies [4], and injuries to bone [1,5]. Athletic injuries can
23	                                         be challenging to treat in-season, with unpredictable healing times following treatment
24	                                         interventions. Surgical management is typically reserved for off-season athletes, as recovery
25	                                         commonly requires a substantial rehabilitation period of 6 to 9 months post-operatively [4].
26	                                         Identifying methods to treat injuries that exert positive clinical effects within 3 months

100	                            Corticosteroids and Platelet-Rich Plasma?
101	                                 Corticosteroid injections may offer rapid relief, but may increase the risk of atrophy,
102	                            pain, and tendon or soft tissue rupture [22]. Furthermore, needle injection therapies in an
103	                            athlete have potential complications, including infection, bleeding, increased pain, and
104	                            prolonged recovery time [22,23]. Unlike these interventions, athletes may continue activities
105	                            as tolerated with ESWT [24]. R-SWT for acute muscle injuries was tolerated well by elite

107	                            F-SWT alone was not shown to be beneficial in jumping athletes, the athletes continued

                                   quality studies should aim to capture larger cohorts of athletes as well as early outcomes
                                   such as 3 and 6 weeks, not limited to outcomes 12 weeks or beyond that have been
                                   commonly reported. ESWT should also be considered an adjunctive tool for managing
                                   commonly encountered athletic injuries. Future research will explore its combination with
                                   orthobiologics to help with perioperative and post-operative recovery, including anterior
                                   cruciate ligament reconstruction [35].

                                   Conclusions
                                        ESWT offers the potential to accelerate recovery from athletic injury and save athletic
                                   clubs valuable resources. Further human athlete studies using ESWT on larger cohorts are
                                   needed to explore optimal indications, dosing, and frequency parameters.

Valid-but-invalid athletes scored lower on Verbal Memory, Visual Memory and Visual Motor Speed, and higher on Reaction Time, at first baseline.",

The abstract reports 769 athletes and about 16% flagged, while the results analyse 760 athletes and give 14.7% (112/760) and 13% (98/760); the counts conflict and this is noted in limitations.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the roughly 15% low-score rate as a general measure of how often baselines are wrong, when it comes from one university, one test version and a retest pattern that may reflect practice or effort rather than true ability.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Walton SR, Broshek DK, Freeman JR, Cullum CM, Resch JE. Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT Baseline Performance in University Athletes. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2018;50(7):1377-1384.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000001592",
  "abstract": "Baseline ImPACT was given to 769 university athletes. Athletes scoring below the 16th percentile on any composite were retested up to two more times. Nine tests (1%) were invalid, and 14.6% had a composite score below the 16th percentile despite passing validity checks. After one retest, 71.4% of those athletes reached the 16th percentile or higher, and 88% did so after a third test.",
  "tldr": "About 1% of ImPACT baselines were invalid, and about 15% had a low composite score that still passed ImPACT's validity checks. Most low scores rose on retest, so a low baseline should be repeated before it is used as the comparison point after injury.",
  "methods": "Baseline ImPACT was given to Division I student-athletes in groups of no more than two, with an athletic trainer trained in ImPACT administering the test. Athletes with any composite below the 16th percentile were retested no earlier than 7 days later, and up to a third time if still low. Composite scores across baseline 1, 2 and 3 were compared with paired t-tests and ImPACT's reliable change index.",
  "findings": "Of 769 records, 9 were flagged invalid by ImPACT. Of the 760 valid profiles, 112 (14.7%) had at least one composite below the 16th percentile at baseline 1. Of those, 80 (71.4%) reached the 16th percentile or higher on baseline 2, and 18 of the 32 still low at baseline 2 did so at baseline 3. The valid-but-invalid group improved significantly on Verbal Memory, Visual Memory, Visual Motor Speed and Reaction Time across retests.",
  "limitations": "Single university, no stand-alone measure of effort, and no record of prior ImPACT exposure. The reported counts conflict: the abstract gives 769 athletes and about 16% flagged, while the results analyse 760 athletes with 14.7% (112/760) and 13% (98/760) low. Many retests fell during the season, so training effects cannot be excluded.",
  "practicalImplications": "Check ImPACT's validity indicators and composite percentiles at baseline. When any composite falls below the 16th percentile, repeat the test before accepting that baseline as the comparison point.",
  "athleteDev": "Run baseline cognitive testing in a controlled, proctored session. Repeat any low composite before accepting it as the athlete's baseline, since many first low scores rose on retest.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to return to sport only through the baseline comparison after a concussion. The study cannot show whether any individual baseline is accurate, so it cannot support a return-to-play decision on its own."
 }
}

Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT Baseline
Performance in University Athletes


                                                                                                                                                      CLINICAL SCIENCES
SAMUEL R. WALTON1, DONNA K. BROSHEK2, JASON R. FREEMAN3, C. MUNRO CULLUM4, and JACOB E. RESCH1
1
  Department of Kinesiology, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA; 2Department of Psychiatry and Neurobehavioral

                                                                       ABSTRACT
          WALTON, S. R., D. K. BROSHEK, J. R. FREEMAN, C. M. CULLUM, and J. E. RESCH. Valid but Invalid: Suboptimal ImPACT
          Baseline Performance in University Athletes. Med. Sci. Sports Exerc., Vol. 50, No. 7, pp. 1377–1384, 2018. Purpose: This study aimed to
          investigate the frequency of valid yet suboptimal Immediate Postconcussion Assessment and Cognitive Test (ImPACT) performance in
          university athletes and to explore the benefit of subsequent ImPACT administrations. Methods: This descriptive laboratory study
          involved baseline administration of ImPACT to 769 university athletes per the institution_s concussion management protocol. Testing
          was proctored in groups of e2 participants. Participants who scored below the 16th percentile according to ImPACT normative data were
          readministered the ImPACT test up to two additional times because these scores were thought to be potentially indicative of suboptimal
          effort or poor understanding of instructions. Descriptive analyses were used to examine validity indicators and individual Verbal and
          Visual Memory, Visual Motor Speed, and Reaction Time ImPACT composite scores in initial and subsequent administrations. Results:
          On the basis of ImPACT_s validity criteria, 1% (9/769) of administrations were invalid and 14.6% (112/769) had one or more composite
          score of G16th percentile but were considered valid. After one readministration, 71.4% (80/112) achieved scores of Q16th percentile
          and an additional 18 of 32 scored Q16th percentile after a third administration. Verbal Memory was most commonly G16th percentile on
          the first administration (43%), Verbal Memory and Visual Motor Speed on the second administration (44% each), and Visual Motor
          Speed alone on the third administration (50%). Conclusions: Approximately 16% of ImPACT records were flagged as invalid or had
          one or more composite scores of G16th percentile, potentially indicative of suboptimal performance. Upon readministration, 88% of those
          participants scored 916th percentile. Clinicians must be aware of suboptimal ImPACT performance as it limits the clinical utility of the
          baseline assessment. Further research is needed to address factors leading to ‘‘valid’’ but invalid baseline performance. Key Words:

Validation of a Composite Outcome Score
for Assessing Return to Sports After
Achilles Tendon Repair
Ronny Lopes,*y MD, Kinan Freiha,z MD , Michael R. Carmont,§ MD, Eugénie Valentin,z
Kylian Alvino,|| PT, Mohamed Mousa,z MD , Gauthier Rauline,z PT,
Francxois Fourchet,{# PT, PhD, Brice Picot,#** PT, PhD , and Alexandre Hardy,z MD, PhD
Investigation performed at Centre Orthopédique Santy, Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz,
Ramsay Santé, Lyon, France
Background: The Ankle-GO is a composite outcome score based on 4 functional tests and 2 patient-reported outcome meas-
ures. It was initially described and validated for its ability to predict return to sports (RTS) at the same level of play after lateral
ankle sprains.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The main aim of this study was to assess the psychometric properties of the Ankle-GO in patients after
Achilles tendon repair. The second objective was to evaluate its ability to predict RTS at the same level of play. It was hypoth-
esized that this composite outcome score is a valid and reliable tool that is able to discriminate and predict the level of RTS at 9
months after Achilles tendon repair.
Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: This was a prospective multicenter study. Patients who were active in sports and underwent primary acute Achilles
tendon repair between April 2021 and December 2022 were included. A control group comprising 30 participants with no history
of lower limb injuries was also evaluated. After standard rehabilitation for the first 2 months, the Ankle-GO was administered at 6
and 9 months after repair by the same experienced physical therapist. During testing, the patients were asked whether they were
able to practice their main sport again and, if so, whether at the same or a lower level of play. A comparison between control
participants and patients at 9 months after surgery was performed.
Results: A total of 50 patients (24 women and 26 men), with a mean age of 38.3 6 10.1 years, were included. No patients were
lost to follow-up at 9 months. The Ankle-GO score at 6 months was 10.7 6 4.8. At 9 months, the score had risen by 4.8 points. All
participants scored above the minimum threshold. The minimum score achieved was 3 points (n = 5 [10%]). Only 1 patient (2%)
obtained the maximum score (25 points). There was a significant difference in the Ankle-GO score between patients at 6 and 9
months and between control participants and patients at 9 months after Achilles tendon repair. Of the 50 patients included in the
study, 14 (28%) returned to their preinjury level of sport at 9 months. The ability of the Ankle-GO score at 6 months to predict RTS
at the preinjury level at 9 months was good (area under the curve = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.56-0.85]; P \ .01). A Youden index of 0.42 was
observed for a cut-off score of 8 points, which corresponds to a sensitivity of 81.8% and a specificity of 41.2%.
Conclusion: The Ankle-GO is a valid tool to evaluate and discriminate patients during the RTS continuum after Achilles tendon
repair and to predict RTS at the same level at 9 months after surgery. This composite outcome score assesses ankle function and
the patient’s psychological readiness to avoid premature RTS and worsening of the injury. Further studies are needed to assess
its value in identifying and predicting patients at risk of a recurrence.
Keywords: Achilles tendon rupture; Achilles tendon repair; return to sports; Ankle-GO; psychological readiness

Validation of a Composite Outcome Score
for Assessing Return to Sports After
Achilles Tendon Repair
Ronny Lopes,*y MD, Kinan Freiha,z MD , Michael R. Carmont,§ MD, Eugénie Valentin,z
Kylian Alvino,|| PT, Mohamed Mousa,z MD , Gauthier Rauline,z PT,
Francxois Fourchet,{# PT, PhD, Brice Picot,#** PT, PhD , and Alexandre Hardy,z MD, PhD
Investigation performed at Centre Orthopédique Santy, Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz,
Ramsay Santé, Lyon, France
Background: The Ankle-GO is a composite outcome score based on 4 functional tests and 2 patient-reported outcome meas-
ures. It was initially described and validated for its ability to predict return to sports (RTS) at the same level of play after lateral
ankle sprains.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The main aim of this study was to assess the psychometric properties of the Ankle-GO in patients after
Achilles tendon repair. The second objective was to evaluate its ability to predict RTS at the same level of play. It was hypoth-
esized that this composite outcome score is a valid and reliable tool that is able to discriminate and predict the level of RTS at 9
months after Achilles tendon repair.
Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: This was a prospective multicenter study. Patients who were active in sports and underwent primary acute Achilles
tendon repair between April 2021 and December 2022 were included. A control group comprising 30 participants with no history
of lower limb injuries was also evaluated. After standard rehabilitation for the first 2 months, the Ankle-GO was administered at 6
and 9 months after repair by the same experienced physical therapist. During testing, the patients were asked whether they were
able to practice their main sport again and, if so, whether at the same or a lower level of play. A comparison between control
participants and patients at 9 months after surgery was performed.
Results: A total of 50 patients (24 women and 26 men), with a mean age of 38.3 6 10.1 years, were included. No patients were
lost to follow-up at 9 months. The Ankle-GO score at 6 months was 10.7 6 4.8. At 9 months, the score had risen by 4.8 points. All
participants scored above the minimum threshold. The minimum score achieved was 3 points (n = 5 [10%]). Only 1 patient (2%)
obtained the maximum score (25 points). There was a significant difference in the Ankle-GO score between patients at 6 and 9
months and between control participants and patients at 9 months after Achilles tendon repair. Of the 50 patients included in the
study, 14 (28%) returned to their preinjury level of sport at 9 months. The ability of the Ankle-GO score at 6 months to predict RTS
at the preinjury level at 9 months was good (area under the curve = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.56-0.85]; P \ .01). A Youden index of 0.42 was
observed for a cut-off score of 8 points, which corresponds to a sensitivity of 81.8% and a specificity of 41.2%.
Conclusion: The Ankle-GO is a valid tool to evaluate and discriminate patients during the RTS continuum after Achilles tendon
repair and to predict RTS at the same level at 9 months after surgery. This composite outcome score assesses ankle function and
the patient’s psychological readiness to avoid premature RTS and worsening of the injury. Further studies are needed to assess
its value in identifying and predicting patients at risk of a recurrence.
Keywords: Achilles tendon rupture; Achilles tendon repair; return to sports; Ankle-GO; psychological readiness

  "doi": "10.7575/aiac.ijkss.v.8n.4p.1",
  "abstract": "The Strive Sense3 smart-textile sEMG system was compared with a research-grade Noraxon system for rectus femoris activity during back squats at 30%, 60% and 80% of estimated 1RM in 17 participants. 35	  Received: August 02, 2020  enabled the measurement of muscle activity using smart textiles. Objective: In this study,

48	  and “Poor to Moderate” to “Excellent” reliability, with a majority of trials achieving “Good” or
49	  better results across all loads [93% trials: r >= 0.7; 87% trials: lower ICC 95% CI bound >= 0.75
50	  (absolute sEMG); 98% trials: lower ICC 95% CI bound >= 0.75 (normalized sEMG)]. Higher
51	  validity and reliability for medium and heavy loads were observed in comparison to the light
52	  load, and several outliers indicate the need for coaches to lubricate sensors and ensure proper
53	  fit to collect accurate data. Conclusion: Examining results alongside practitioner feedback
54	  indicate the StriveTM Sense3 system is capable of tracking sEMG activity in comparison to a
55	  research-grade system.

  Article history  Background: Recent innovations in surface electromyographic (sEMG) technology have
  Received: August 02, 2020  enabled the measurement of muscle activity using smart textiles. Objective: In this study,
  Accepted: October 06, 2020  the StriveTM Sense3 performance monitoring system is evaluated against a research-grade
  Published: October 31, 2020  system, NoraxonTM, in measuring activity during the back squat exercise. Method: Seventeen
  Volume: 8 Issue: 4  participants performed three total trials of the squat exercise with a progressive load for
  individual trials equal to 30%, 60%, and 80% of their estimated maximum 1RM (one-repetition
  Conflicts of interest: None.  maximum). sEMG measurements from the rectus femoris were captured for the left and

  and interrater reliability of the StriveTM Sense3 device. Additionally, five coaches at the
  agencies in the public, commercial, or

  not-for-profit sectors.
  to the findings from this study. Results: Results ranged from “Poor” to “Excellent” validity
  and “Poor to Moderate” to “Excellent” reliability, with a majority of trials achieving “Good” or
  better results across all loads [93% trials: r >= 0.7; 87% trials: lower ICC 95% CI bound >= 0.75
  (absolute sEMG); 98% trials: lower ICC 95% CI bound >= 0.75 (normalized sEMG)]. Higher
  validity and reliability for medium and heavy loads were observed in comparison to the light
  load, and several outliers indicate the need for coaches to lubricate sensors and ensure proper
  fit to collect accurate data. Conclusion: Examining results alongside practitioner feedback
  indicate the StriveTM Sense3 system is capable of tracking sEMG activity in comparison to a
  research-grade system.

  ABSTRACT
  Consumer-­grade optical heart rate (HR) sensors emerged as promising tools to monitor volume and intensity of physical ac-
  tivity (PA). However, no validation study of optical HR sensors included recent comprehensive validation recommendations,
  required for facilitating usage for medical purposes. Validity of HR data measured with four consumer-­grade optical sensors, the
  wrist-­worn Garmin Venu 2S and Polar Vantage M2, and the upper arm-­worn Polar Verity Sense and Scosche Rhythm24 were
  assessed in 32 participants over 24 h including various laboratory-­based and free-­living activities. Furthermore, validity of time
  at moderate or vigorous PA intensity zones was analyzed. A medical-­grade ECG served as a reference. Reliability was assessed
  by analyzing data of laboratory-­based activities during two visits. Across activities, the mean absolute percentage error ranged
  from 2.2% to 4.7% and intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.91 to 0.98, indicating high validity for all optical sensors.
  All sensors validly detected time spent at moderate or vigorous intensities (mean error < 10%), except Polar M2 for moderate PA
  (mean error 12.8%) and Garmin V2 for vigorous PA (mean error −15.9%). Sensor day-­to-­day reliability was high, indicated by a
  mean absolute error of < 5 beats/min. Upper arm-­worn sensors consistently outperformed wrist-­worn sensors, particularly in ac-
  tivities involving increased arm movement and at higher intensities. Our findings identified an overall high validity of these four
  consumer-­grade optical HR sensors, also for assessing time spent at higher PA intensities. However, differences were observed
  between sensors regarding activity subtypes and intensity levels. These data support informed decisions when selecting optical
  sensors for PA monitoring and intervention.

15	  ABSTRACT
16	  Consumer-­grade optical heart rate (HR) sensors emerged as promising tools to monitor volume and intensity of physical ac-
17	  tivity (PA). However, no validation study of optical HR sensors included recent comprehensive validation recommendations,
18	  required for facilitating usage for medical purposes. Validity of HR data measured with four consumer-­grade optical sensors, the
19	  wrist-­worn Garmin Venu 2S and Polar Vantage M2, and the upper arm-­worn Polar Verity Sense and Scosche Rhythm24 were
20	  assessed in 32 participants over 24 h including various laboratory-­based and free-­living activities. Furthermore, validity of time
21	  at moderate or vigorous PA intensity zones was analyzed. A medical-­grade ECG served as a reference. Reliability was assessed
22	  by analyzing data of laboratory-­based activities during two visits. Across activities, the mean absolute percentage error ranged
23	  from 2.2% to 4.7% and intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.91 to 0.98, indicating high validity for all optical sensors.
24	  All sensors validly detected time spent at moderate or vigorous intensities (mean error < 10%), except Polar M2 for moderate PA
25	  (mean error 12.8%) and Garmin V2 for vigorous PA (mean error −15.9%). Sensor day-­to-­day reliability was high, indicated by a
26	  mean absolute error of < 5 beats/min. Upper arm-­worn sensors consistently outperformed wrist-­worn sensors, particularly in ac-
27	  tivities involving increased arm movement and at higher intensities. Our findings identified an overall high validity of these four
28	  consumer-­grade optical HR sensors, also for assessing time spent at higher PA intensities. However, differences were observed
29	  between sensors regarding activity subtypes and intensity levels. These data support informed decisions when selecting optical
30	  sensors for PA monitoring and intervention.

Validity of Four Consumer-­Grade Optical Heart Rate
Sensors for Assessing Volume and Intensity Distribution of
Physical Activity
Michael Neudorfer1  | Devender Kumar2  | Jan David Smeddinck 2  | Stefan Tino Kulnik 2 | Josef Niebauer1,2,3 |
Gunnar Treff 2,3  | Mahdi Sareban1,2

Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria

Received: 27 June 2024 | Revised: 4 September 2024 | Accepted: 14 October 2024
Funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.
Keywords: Garmin | mHealth | physical activity | physical medicine and rehabilitation | polar | telemedicine | validation | wearables
  ABSTRACT
  Consumer-­grade optical heart rate (HR) sensors emerged as promising tools to monitor volume and intensity of physical ac-
  tivity (PA). However, no validation study of optical HR sensors included recent comprehensive validation recommendations,
  required for facilitating usage for medical purposes. Validity of HR data measured with four consumer-­grade optical sensors, the
  wrist-­worn Garmin Venu 2S and Polar Vantage M2, and the upper arm-­worn Polar Verity Sense and Scosche Rhythm24 were
  assessed in 32 participants over 24 h including various laboratory-­based and free-­living activities. Furthermore, validity of time
  at moderate or vigorous PA intensity zones was analyzed. A medical-­grade ECG served as a reference. Reliability was assessed
  by analyzing data of laboratory-­based activities during two visits. Across activities, the mean absolute percentage error ranged
  from 2.2% to 4.7% and intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.91 to 0.98, indicating high validity for all optical sensors.
  All sensors validly detected time spent at moderate or vigorous intensities (mean error < 10%), except Polar M2 for moderate PA
  (mean error 12.8%) and Garmin V2 for vigorous PA (mean error −15.9%). Sensor day-­to-­day reliability was high, indicated by a
  mean absolute error of < 5 beats/min. Upper arm-­worn sensors consistently outperformed wrist-­worn sensors, particularly in ac-
  tivities involving increased arm movement and at higher intensities. Our findings identified an overall high validity of these four
  consumer-­grade optical HR sensors, also for assessing time spent at higher PA intensities. However, differences were observed
  between sensors regarding activity subtypes and intensity levels. These data support informed decisions when selecting optical
  sensors for PA monitoring and intervention.
  Trial Registration: The study was performed in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its current amendments and
  was prospectively registered at Clini​calTr​ials.​gov (ID NCT05525000).

 "sourceFile": "Validity of force-velocity profiling assessed with a pneumatic leg press device.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'Validity of Force-Velocity Profiling Assessed With a Pneumatic Leg Press Device' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": [
  "Monitoring & Technology",
  "Training & Performance"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Performance",
  "Research & Analytics",
  "Athletic Training"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Adult / Recreational"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Concurrent validity study of force-velocity variables from five Keiser pneumatic leg press units, compared with two force plates and a linear encoder, in 14 regularly active adults (mean age 29 years, 82 kg). Across 997 repetitions, average and peak force and velocity had correlations of 0.994 to 0.999 and coefficients of variation of 1.5% to 8.6%. Theoretical F0, V0, Pmax and force-velocity slope had correlations of 0.983 to 0.997 and coefficients of variation of 1.4% to 5.9%, while single-repetition power was less precise (CV 11.6% average, 17.2% peak).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Fourteen participants, with sex not reported, tested on one leg press model at Norwegian sports centres. The reference is device measurement (force plates and encoder), not athlete outcomes, so the paper does not show that profile values predict performance or change with training. The abstract gives a systematic bias of 0.7% to 7.1%, while the results give -8.4% to 4.7%; both are reported and the conflict is noted.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Good agreement across Keiser units does not make the values interchangeable with force-plate values or with vertical jump profiles, and single-repetition power should not be compared directly between athletes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2021,
  "citation": "Lindberg K, Eythorsdottir I, Solberg P, Gløersen Ø, Seynnes O, Bjørnsen T, et al. Validity of Force-Velocity Profiling Assessed With a Pneumatic Leg Press Device. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021 (ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2020-0954",
  "abstract": "Concurrent validity of force-velocity variables from five Keiser leg press devices was tested against two force plates and a linear encoder in 14 participants across 997 repetitions. Average and peak force and velocity agreed closely with reference measures. Extrapolated theoretical maximal force, velocity and power were precise, while single-repetition power was less precise. The authors recommend theoretical maximal power over single-repetition power.",
  "tldr": "Keiser pneumatic leg press data agreed closely with force plates and a linear encoder. The force-velocity profile (F0, V0, Pmax, slope) was more precise than single-repetition power, so use theoretical Pmax when profiling on this device.",
  "methods": "Fourteen regularly active participants completed 997 leg press repetitions across five Keiser units, with two force plates and a linear encoder recording at the same time. Protocol 1 used submaximal loads from 25 to 450 kgf in 14 participants; protocol 2 used maximal efforts across the Keiser 10-step test in 11 participants. Force-velocity profiles were fitted by linear regression for each participant and compared with reference data using bias, CV, correlation and ICC.",
  "findings": "Average and peak force and velocity correlated at 0.994 to 0.999 with coefficients of variation of 1.5% to 8.6%, and most biases were trivial to small. Average and peak power had CVs of 11.6% and 17.2%. Theoretical F0, V0, Pmax and slope had CVs of 1.4% to 5.9%. Deviations between the five devices were trivial.",
  "limitations": "Only 14 participants, with sex not reported, using one leg press model across five units at one sports centre. The abstract's bias range (0.7% to 7.1%) differs from the results (-8.4% to 4.7%). Submaximal and maximal efforts were analysed separately, and results may not transfer to other devices.",
  "practicalImplications": "When profiling athletes on the Keiser pneumatic leg press, use theoretical maximal power (Pmax) and the F0 and V0 intercepts from the regression rather than single-repetition power. Keep the same unit when comparing an athlete over time, because device differences were trivial but not zero.",
  "athleteDev": "Use the force-velocity profile (F0, V0, Pmax, slope) from the pneumatic leg press to monitor training change, with theoretical Pmax as the power measure. The CVs of 1.4% to 5.9% give a reference for whether a change is larger than measurement noise.",
  "rtp": "The study has no injured participants and no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot be used to judge strength or readiness after injury."
 }
}

  Validity of Force–Velocity Proﬁling Assessed
  With a Pneumatic Leg Press Device
  Kolbjørn Lindberg, Ingrid Eythorsdottir, Paul Solberg, Øyvind Gløersen,
  Olivier Seynnes, Thomas Bjørnsen, and Gøran Paulsen
  Purpose: The aim of this study was to examine the concurrent validity of force–velocity (FV) variables assessed across 5 Keiser
  leg press devices. Methods: A linear encoder and 2 independent force plates (MuscleLab devices) were mounted on each of the 5
  leg press devices. A total of 997 leg press executions, covering a wide range of forces and velocities, were performed by 14
  participants (29 [7] y, 181 [5] cm, 82 [8] kg) across the 5 devices. Average and peak force, velocity, and power values were
  collected simultaneously from the Keiser and MuscleLab devices for each repetition. Individual FV proﬁles were ﬁtted to each
  participant from peak and average force and velocity measurements. Theoretical maximal force, velocity, and power were
  deduced from the FV relationship. Results: Average and peak force and velocity had a coefﬁcient of variation of 1.5% to 8.6%,
  near-perfect correlations (.994–.999), and a systematic bias of 0.7% to 7.1% when compared with reference measurements.
  Average and peak power showed larger coefﬁcient of variations (11.6% and 17.2%), despite excellent correlations (.977 and
  .952), and trivial to small biases (3.9% and 8.4%). Extrapolated FV variables showed near-perfect correlations (.983–.997) with
  trivial to small biases (1.4%–11.2%) and a coefﬁcient of variation of 1.4% to 5.9%. Conclusions: The Keiser leg press device can
  obtain valid measurements over a wide range of forces and velocities across different devices. To accurately measure power,
  theoretical maximal power calculated from the FV proﬁle is recommended over average and peak power values from single
  repetitions, due to the lower random error observed for theoretical maximal power.

Team Physician’s Corner
Validity of Research Based on Public
Data in Sports Medicine
A Quantitative Assessment of Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Injuries in the National Football League
Paul M. Inclan,* MD, Peter S. Chang,* MD, Christina D. Mack,y PhD,
Gary S. Solomon,z§ PhD, Robert H. Brophy,* MD, Richard Y. Hinton,|| MD, PT,
Kurt P. Spindler,{ MD, Allen K. Sills,z§ MD, and Matthew J. Matava,*# MD
Investigation performed at Washington University in Saint Louis, Missouri, USA
Background: Numerous researchers have leveraged publicly available Internet sources to publish publicly obtained data (POD)
studies concerning various orthopaedic injuries in National Football League (NFL) players.
Purpose: To provide a comprehensive systematic review of all POD studies regarding musculoskeletal injuries in NFL athletes
and to use anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries in NFL players to quantify the percentage of injuries identified by these studies.
Study Design: Systematic review; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted to identify all published studies utilizing POD regarding ACL injury in NFL athletes
from 2000 to 2019. Data regarding player demographics were extracted from each publication. These results were compared with
prospectively collected data reported by the teams’ medical staff to the NFL Injury Surveillance System database linked to the
League’s electronic health record. An ACL ‘‘capture rate’’ for each article was calculated by dividing the number of ACL injuries
in the POD study by the total number of ACL injuries in the NFL injury database occurring in the study period of interest.
Results: A total of 42 studies were extracted that met the definition of a POD study: 28 evaluated a variety of injuries and 14 dealt
specifically with ACL injuries, with 35 (83%) of the 42 studies published during or since 2015. POD studies captured a mean of
66% (range, 31%-90%) of ACL injuries reported by the teams’ medical staff. This inability to capture all injury rates varied by
position, with 86% capture of ACL injuries in skill athletes, 72% in midskill athletes, and 61% in linemen. POD studies captured
35% of injuries occurring during special teams play.
Conclusion: The frequency of studies leveraging publicly obtained injury data in NFL players has rapidly increased since 2000.
There is significant heterogeneity in the degree to which POD studies correctly identify ACL injuries from public reports. Sports
medicine research relying solely on publicly obtained sources should be interpreted with an understanding of their inherent lim-
itations and biases. These studies underreport the true incidence of injuries, with a bias toward capturing injuries in more popular
players.

Validity of Research Based on Public
Data in Sports Medicine
A Quantitative Assessment of Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Injuries in the National Football League
Paul M. Inclan,* MD, Peter S. Chang,* MD, Christina D. Mack,y PhD,
Gary S. Solomon,z§ PhD, Robert H. Brophy,* MD, Richard Y. Hinton,|| MD, PT,
Kurt P. Spindler,{ MD, Allen K. Sills,z§ MD, and Matthew J. Matava,*# MD
Investigation performed at Washington University in Saint Louis, Missouri, USA
Background: Numerous researchers have leveraged publicly available Internet sources to publish publicly obtained data (POD)
studies concerning various orthopaedic injuries in National Football League (NFL) players.
Purpose: To provide a comprehensive systematic review of all POD studies regarding musculoskeletal injuries in NFL athletes
and to use anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries in NFL players to quantify the percentage of injuries identified by these studies.
Study Design: Systematic review; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted to identify all published studies utilizing POD regarding ACL injury in NFL athletes
from 2000 to 2019. Data regarding player demographics were extracted from each publication. These results were compared with
prospectively collected data reported by the teams’ medical staff to the NFL Injury Surveillance System database linked to the
League’s electronic health record. An ACL ‘‘capture rate’’ for each article was calculated by dividing the number of ACL injuries
in the POD study by the total number of ACL injuries in the NFL injury database occurring in the study period of interest.
Results: A total of 42 studies were extracted that met the definition of a POD study: 28 evaluated a variety of injuries and 14 dealt
specifically with ACL injuries, with 35 (83%) of the 42 studies published during or since 2015. POD studies captured a mean of
66% (range, 31%-90%) of ACL injuries reported by the teams’ medical staff. This inability to capture all injury rates varied by
position, with 86% capture of ACL injuries in skill athletes, 72% in midskill athletes, and 61% in linemen. POD studies captured
35% of injuries occurring during special teams play.
Conclusion: The frequency of studies leveraging publicly obtained injury data in NFL players has rapidly increased since 2000.
There is significant heterogeneity in the degree to which POD studies correctly identify ACL injuries from public reports. Sports
medicine research relying solely on publicly obtained sources should be interpreted with an understanding of their inherent lim-
itations and biases. These studies underreport the true incidence of injuries, with a bias toward capturing injuries in more popular
players.

{
 "id": "Q42",
 "sourceFile": "Validity of the Elite HRV Smart      Phone app for examining heart rate variability in a field based      setting.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Manuscript title 'Validity of the Elite HRV Smart Phone Application for Examining Heart Rate Variability in a Field Based Setting' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": [
  "Monitoring & Technology",
  "Recovery & Readiness"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Performance",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Research & Analytics",
  "Coaching"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Male Athletes",
  "Female Athletes",
  "Adult / Recreational"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Validation of the Elite HRV smartphone app against Kubios HRV 2.2 for log-transformed resting rMSSD, using R-R intervals from a Polar H7 recorded on waking for 14 consecutive days in 37 recreational athletes (29 men, 8 women; mean age 30.8 years) living in a dormitory. The two measures correlated strongly (r = 0.92, 95% CI 0.90 to 0.93), with a mean bias of -2.7% and 6.4% of residuals outside the limits of agreement (-12.0% to 7.0%). The authors conclude the app is not valid against Kubios.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Recording length varied beyond the planned 10 minutes because some participants lost track of time, and the app cannot select or trim segments, which the authors suggest may explain the disagreement. Only one heart rate monitor and one reference software were used, with no reliability testing. The sample was young, mostly male recreational athletes, so findings may not transfer to elite or female athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "A strong correlation (r = 0.92) does not mean the app's values match Kubios, because the bias and the wide limits of agreement mean the two cannot be used interchangeably.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2017,
  "citation": "Perrotta AS, Jeklin A, Hives BA, Meanwell LE, Warburton DER. Validity of the Elite HRV Smart Phone Application for Examining Heart Rate Variability in a Field Based Setting. J Strength Cond Res. 2017 (ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1519/JSC.0000000000001841",
  "abstract": "R-R intervals were recorded on waking for 14 days with the Elite HRV app and exported to Kubios HRV 2.2 for analysis. The app and Kubios rMSSD (log) correlated at r = 0.92, with a bias of -2.7% and 6.4% of residuals outside the limits of agreement. The authors judged the app not valid, and suggested it may be reliable rather than valid.",
  "tldr": "The Elite HRV app's rMSSD correlated strongly with Kubios (r = 0.92), but it read about 3% lower on average and 6% of readings fell outside the limits of agreement. The authors judged it not valid against Kubios and suggested it might be reliable, which this study did not test.",
  "methods": "Thirty-seven recreational athletes (29 men, 8 women; age 30.8 +/- 11.7 years) lived in a dormitory for 14 days and recorded resting R-R intervals with a Polar H7 on waking for about 10 minutes. Recordings were analysed in the Elite HRV app and exported to Kubios HRV 2.2. Log rMSSD from the two sources was compared by Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis.",
  "findings": "The app and Kubios correlated at r = 0.92 (95% CI 0.90 to 0.93, P < 0.0001). The mean bias was -2.7% (95% CI -3.1 to -2.3%), with limits of agreement of -12.0% to 7.0% and 6.4% of residuals outside them. The authors state that the bias CI did not include the line of equality.",
  "limitations": "One heart rate monitor and one reference software were used, with no reliability testing. Recording durations varied beyond 10 minutes and the app cannot trim recordings. The sample was young and mostly male recreational athletes, so results may not transfer to elite or female athletes.",
  "practicalImplications": "Do not treat Elite HRV rMSSD values as interchangeable with Kubios values. Record for a fixed duration, as the authors advise, because variable recording lengths added to the disagreement.",
  "athleteDev": "Use this app's morning HRV readings with caution, since they run about 3% below Kubios on average with wide limits of agreement (-12% to +7%). Keep recordings to a fixed 10 minutes to reduce error.",
  "rtp": "The study addresses HRV measurement agreement in healthy recreational athletes. It does not assess injured or returning athletes and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}

efficient and practical when monitoring athletes in a team setting as the app is capable of
collecting, analyzing and exporting vagal related HRV indexes directly to the practitioner for
further examination and recording. The ability to analyze, store and export HRV recordings may
be most practical for non-centralized athletes and with teams travelling with minimal staff. This
option would allow for the continuing physiological support from practitioners not traveling
provided internet access is available for exporting data. In conjunction with the level of validity a
sport science assessment tool offers, its ability to remain reliable may be equally as important as

multiple times should be of great important to the integrative support staff when desiring to

instruments commonly elicit larger sampling errors as the value being measured increases (19),
an issue that may become problematic when measuring large HRV values. However, the

uniformity of error whereby applying a similar magnitude of error for all values measured (12).
